standalone-proof-types.text: A form of identification issued consistent with the requirements of the REAL ID Act of 2005 that indicates the applicant is a citizen of the United States.
The applicant's official United States military identification card, together with a United States military record of service showing that the applicant's place of birth was in the United States.
A valid government-issued photo identification card issued by a Federal, State or Tribal government showing that the applicant's place of birth was in the United States.

anchor-photo-id-types.text: A valid government-issued photo identification card issued by a Federal, State or Tribal government other than an identification described in paragraphs (1) through (4).

supporting-document-types.text: A certified birth certificate issued by a State, a unit of local government in a State, or a Tribal government which-- [clauses (i)-(vii)]
An extract from a United States hospital Record of Birth created at the time of the applicant's birth which indicates that the applicant's place of birth was in the United States.
A final adoption decree showing the applicant's name and that the applicant's place of birth was in the United States.
A Consular Report of Birth Abroad of a citizen of the United States or a certification of the applicant's Report of Birth of a United States citizen issued by the Secretary of State.

A Naturalization Certificate or Certificate of Citizenship issued by the Secretary of Homeland Security or any other document or method of proof of United States citizenship issued by the Federal government pursuant to the Immigration and Nationality Act.
An American Indian Card issued by the Department of Homeland Security with the classification 'KIC'.

valid-photo-id-types.text: A valid State-issued motor vehicle driver's license that includes a photo of the individual and an expiration date.
A valid State-issued identification card that includes a photo of the individual and an expiration date issued by a State motor vehicle authority.
A valid United States passport for the individual.
A valid military identification for the individual.
A valid identification document issued by a Tribal government that includes a photo of the individual and an expiration date.

religious-objection-affidavit-types.text: an affidavit developed and made available to the individual by the State attesting that the individual does not possess the identification required under subparagraph (A) because the individual has a religious objection to being photographed.

nodes.label: H.R. 22 — SAVE Act
nodes.description: Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, 119th Congress. Passed House 220-208, April 10, 2025.
nodes.why_it_matters: This is the bill being analyzed. Every formal conclusion traces back to its actual text.

nodes.label: NVRA Baseline (52 U.S.C. §§ 20501–20511)
nodes.description: National Voter Registration Act — the statutory baseline that the SAVE Act amends.
nodes.why_it_matters: The NVRA is the existing federal baseline for voter registration. The SAVE Act modifies this framework.

nodes.label: 5th Amendment (Due Process / Equal Protection)
nodes.description: Equal protection component applied to federal action via Bolling v. Sharpe, 347 U.S. 497 (1954). Operative constitutional hook for the model.
nodes.why_it_matters: The 5th Amendment's due process clause is the constitutional hook for challenging unreasonable voting burdens.

nodes.label: 14th Amendment § 1 (Citizenship / Equal Protection)
nodes.description: Defines citizenship and equal protection for state action. Provides the citizenship definition used in voter qualification analysis.

nodes.label: 17th Amendment (Senate Voter Qualifications)
nodes.description: Extends voter qualification framework to Senate elections.
nodes.why_it_matters: The 17th Amendment extended direct election to senators. It reinforces the constitutional right to vote.

nodes.label: 24th Amendment (Poll Tax Prohibition)
nodes.description: Prohibits poll taxes in federal elections. Relevant to whether document-acquisition costs constitute an impermissible tax.

nodes.label: Crawford v. Marion County (2008)
nodes.description: Supreme Court plurality upholding Indiana voter ID law under Anderson-Burdick framework. Key precedent for burden analysis.
nodes.why_it_matters: Crawford v. Marion County is the Supreme Court's controlling framework for evaluating voter ID laws.

nodes.label: Anderson-Burdick Framework
nodes.description: Sliding-scale test: severe burdens trigger strict scrutiny; lesser burdens require only rational basis.
nodes.source_ref: Anderson v. Celebrezze, 460 U.S. 780 (1983); Burdick v. Takushi, 504 U.S. 428 (1992)

nodes.label: Fish v. Kobach (10th Cir. 2016)
nodes.description: Kansas documentary proof-of-citizenship requirement. Found ~18,000 applicants unable to complete registration. Key empirical record.
nodes.why_it_matters: Fish v. Kobach found that strict proof-of-citizenship requirements blocked legitimate voters.

nodes.label: Bolling v. Sharpe (1954)
nodes.description: Reverse incorporation: Fifth Amendment due process includes equal protection component binding the federal government.

nodes.label: source_manifest.json
nodes.description: Registry of 21 authoritative sources with URLs, citations, and local file references.

nodes.label: clause_trace.csv
nodes.description: 38-row mapping from every defaxiom to its authoritative source clause.

nodes.label: ACE Controlled-English Statements
nodes.description: 13 source provisions translated to Attempto Controlled English with predicate targets.

nodes.label: citizen-a is a qualified voter
nodes.description: Scenario ground truth: citizen-a is a U.S. citizen, eligible to vote, of legal age.
nodes.why_it_matters: This ground fact sets up the test scenario: a real citizen, eligible to vote, who wants to register.

nodes.label: citizen-a lacks qualifying documents
nodes.description: citizen-a does not possess any of the qualifying documents listed in the SAVE Act (no REAL ID, passport, birth certificate, etc.).
nodes.why_it_matters: The critical scenario fact: the citizen does not have any qualifying documents, which triggers the SAVE Act's proof requirement.

nodes.label: Voting is a constitutionally protected right
nodes.description: Source-traced from constitutional provisions.
nodes.why_it_matters: Establishes that voting is constitutionally protected — the foundation for any burden analysis.

nodes.label: SAVE Act is a federal law
nodes.description: Source-traced: H.R. 22 is a law regulating voter registration.
nodes.why_it_matters: Grounds the formal analysis in real legislation. Without this, the model would be about a hypothetical law.

nodes.label: Registration attempt is a registration transaction
nodes.description: The act of applying to register constitutes a registration transaction subject to SAVE Act requirements.
nodes.why_it_matters: Classifies the act of registering as a formal transaction subject to the SAVE Act's requirements.

nodes.label: Statute triggers denial for citizen-a
nodes.description: Under the SAVE Act, citizen-a's registration is denied because they lack documentary proof.
nodes.why_it_matters: This is the crux: under the SAVE Act, lacking documents triggers a denial of registration.

nodes.label: Citizen lacks documents through no fault
nodes.description: Challenger-side empirical premise: citizen-a lacks qualifying documents through no personal fault (e.g., born at home in rural area, elderly, records destroyed).
nodes.why_it_matters: HIGH RISK — This empirical claim (the citizen lacks documents through no fault of their own) is the most contestable assumption in the challenger's case. ~18,000 applicants were blocked in Kansas under a similar requirement.

nodes.label: Obtaining documents is materially burdensome
nodes.description: Challenger-side empirical premise: obtaining qualifying documents imposes a material burden (cost, travel, time, bureaucratic barriers).
nodes.why_it_matters: HIGH RISK — The claim that obtaining qualifying documents is materially burdensome. Based on Crawford plurality language, not a holding.

nodes.label: Government: burden is not severe
nodes.description: Government-side empirical premise: the burden of obtaining documents is not severe, and an adequate alternative process exists.
nodes.why_it_matters: HIGH RISK — The government's counter-claim that the documentation burden is not severe. Directly contradicts the challenger's burden claim.

nodes.label: Adequate alternative process exists
nodes.description: Government premise: the § 8(j)(2)(A) attestation process provides an adequate alternative path to registration.
nodes.why_it_matters: The government's argument that the SAVE Act's alternative process provides an adequate safety valve.

nodes.label: Mandatory alternative-process reading
nodes.description: § 8(j)(2)(A): 'sufficiently established' means the official must approve if evidence is adequate → guaranteed path to registration.
nodes.why_it_matters: Government's interpretation: 'shall make a determination' means mandatory approval when evidence meets standards.

nodes.label: Discretionary alternative-process reading
nodes.description: § 8(j)(2)(A): 'sufficiently established' gives the official discretion → possible denial even with evidence → no guaranteed registration path.
nodes.why_it_matters: Challenger's interpretation: 'shall make a determination' means the official may still deny registration.

nodes.label: Election integrity is an important interest
nodes.description: Government doctrinal premise: preventing noncitizen voting is an important or compelling government interest.
nodes.why_it_matters: A doctrinal assumption from Crawford: protecting election integrity is an important government interest.

nodes.label: Requirement is reasonable and evenhanded
nodes.description: Government doctrinal premise: the documentary proof requirement is reasonable, rationally connected to the interest, and evenhanded.
nodes.why_it_matters: A doctrinal claim: the SAVE Act's requirement is reasonable and applies evenhandedly to all applicants.

nodes.label: Severe burden defeats regulation
nodes.description: Challenger doctrinal premise: under Anderson-Burdick, a severe burden on the right to vote makes the regulation constitutionally invalid.
nodes.why_it_matters: Anderson-Burdick doctrine: if a voting regulation imposes a severe burden, it is constitutionally invalid.

nodes.label: Registration State Machine
nodes.description: 10-state, 9-event executable model: :submitted → :pending → :approved → :registered or :denied, with :alt-pending → :alt-approved/:alt-denied alternative path.

nodes.label: Document Recognizer Model
nodes.description: Executable recognizers for REAL ID, passport, military ID, government photo ID, and supporting documents.
nodes.why_it_matters: The document recognizer formally defines which documents satisfy the SAVE Act's proof-of-citizenship requirement.

nodes.label: Burden Derivation Chain (defun)
nodes.description: 5-step executable burden chain: lacks-docs → cannot-obtain → material-burden → severe-burden → invalid-regulation.
nodes.why_it_matters: This 5-step executable chain derives the severity of the burden rather than assuming it, making the conclusion more defensible.

nodes.label: Interpretive Hinge Fork
nodes.description: Encapsulate-based model: § 8(j)(2)(A) 'sufficiently established' splits into mandatory (government) vs. discretionary (challenger) readings.
nodes.why_it_matters: The interpretive fork is the key structural insight: the entire dispute reduces to how one statutory phrase is read.

nodes.label: Existential Propositions (defun-sk)
nodes.description: 4 Skolemized existential claims: exists-burdened-citizen, exists-no-fault-citizen, exists-documentless-eligible-voter, exists-citizen-facing-discretionary-denial.
nodes.why_it_matters: Existential propositions prove that the affected class of voters is non-empty — real people are affected.

nodes.label: Anderson-Burdick Doctrinal Standard
nodes.description: Encapsulate-based doctrinal standard: severe burden → strict scrutiny; not-severe → rational basis.
nodes.why_it_matters: The encapsulated doctrinal standard ensures the Anderson-Burdick test is applied consistently.

nodes.label: Denial derivation
nodes.description: citizen-a's registration is denied because they lack documentary proof and no alternative process is approved.
nodes.why_it_matters: Shows that under the SAVE Act, citizen-a's registration is denied — the denial is a logical consequence of the statute.

nodes.label: Lacks-documents derivation
nodes.description: citizen-a possesses no qualifying document from the SAVE Act list.
nodes.why_it_matters: Formally derives that the citizen has no qualifying document from the SAVE Act's list.

nodes.label: Full burden derivation chain
nodes.description: Executable defun chain: citizen-a-has-material-burden → citizen-a-burden-is-severe → regulation-is-invalid.
nodes.why_it_matters: The burden derivation chain transforms raw facts into the legal conclusion that the burden is severe.

nodes.label: Alternative-process derivation
nodes.description: Under mandatory reading: alternative process provides guaranteed registration path. Under discretionary reading: official may deny.
nodes.why_it_matters: This is where the two models diverge: the mandatory reading provides a path to registration; the discretionary reading does not.

nodes.label: Interpretive hinge fork split
nodes.description: The outcome pivots on whether § 8(j)(2)(A) is read as mandatory approval or discretionary determination.
nodes.why_it_matters: The interpretive hinge fork is the single point where the challenger and government models split. Everything above is shared.

nodes.label: Registration requires a prior acceptance state (documents accepted or alternative process approved)
nodes.description: Registration requires a prior acceptance path through the state machine. 0 axioms.
nodes.why_it_matters: This pure structural theorem proves that registration must pass through an acceptance state. It depends on zero assumptions — genuine process verification.

nodes.label: Denial requires a denial-triggering state (documents rejected, alternative denied, or direct denial)
nodes.description: Denial requires a prior denial path through the state machine. 0 axioms.
nodes.why_it_matters: The denial-side dual: reaching 'denied' requires passing through a denial-triggering state. Zero assumptions.

nodes.label: Registered and denied are final — no later event changes the outcome
nodes.description: Once registered or denied, later events do not change the terminal outcome. 0 axioms.
nodes.why_it_matters: Once registered or denied, the outcome is permanent. This guarantees the state machine has no anomalous loops.

nodes.label: A bundle with no statute-recognized document cannot be documentary proof
nodes.description: A bundle of only nonqualifying documents cannot satisfy documentary proof. 0 axioms.
nodes.why_it_matters: If a citizen's documents are all nonqualifying, they cannot satisfy the documentary proof requirement. Zero assumptions.

nodes.label: With every other precondition fixed, conflict ⇔ the regulation is not valid (the pivot)
nodes.description: The constitutional conflict condition is logically equivalent to (not (valid-regulationp law x)). The entire dispute reduces to this single predicate.
nodes.why_it_matters: The most important structural theorem: the entire constitutional dispute reduces to a single predicate — valid-regulationp. If the regulation is valid, no conflict; if invalid, conflict.

nodes.label: Lacks documents + cannot obtain them + no alternative ⇒ severe burden (derived, not assumed)
nodes.description: Derives: citizen-a faces severe burden → regulation is invalid, using the executable defun chain.
nodes.why_it_matters: Derives the full burden chain: lacking documents + cannot obtain + no alternative → severe burden → invalid regulation. Uses the executable defun chain.

nodes.label: Invalid regulation + qualified voter denied ⇒ constitutional conflict (challenger direction)
nodes.description: If the regulation is not valid, the formal conflict condition is established.
nodes.why_it_matters: If the regulation is not valid, the formal conflict condition is established. The bridge from burden analysis to constitutional conflict.

nodes.label: Valid regulation ⇒ no constitutional conflict, whatever else holds (government direction)
nodes.description: If the regulation is valid, no formal conflict condition exists.
nodes.why_it_matters: If the regulation is valid, the government wins — no formal conflict exists. The government's main defense.

nodes.label: valid-regulationp
nodes.description: The single interpretive/doctrinal predicate that determines the constitutional outcome. Not proved by ACL2 — determined by the assumption set.
nodes.why_it_matters: This single predicate — valid-regulationp — is the constitutional pivot. It is not proved by ACL2; it is determined entirely by which assumptions the user selects.

nodes.label: Challenger: CONSTITUTIONAL CONFLICT
nodes.description: Under challenger assumptions (no-fault, material burden, severe burden, discretionary reading, invalid regulation), ACL2 derives that a formal constitutional conflict exists.
nodes.why_it_matters: Under challenger assumptions (no-fault, material burden, discretionary reading, invalid regulation), ACL2 derives that a formal constitutional conflict exists.

nodes.label: Government: NO CONFLICT
nodes.description: Under government assumptions (burden not severe, adequate alternative, mandatory reading, election integrity, valid regulation), ACL2 derives that no formal constitutional conflict exists.
nodes.why_it_matters: Under government assumptions (burden not severe, adequate alternative, mandatory reading, valid regulation), ACL2 derives that no formal constitutional conflict exists.

nodes.label: Clause IR → ACL2 + ACE + Markdown (4 generated books)
nodes.description: Deterministic JSON IR for enumerated definitions (§ 3(b)), the documentary-proof prohibition, the registration process table, and the § 8(k) removal table. tools/clauses_to_acl2.py compiles each to an ACL2 book, an APE-validated ACE statement, and a Markdown paraphrase; CI fails if any of the three drifts.

nodes.label: § 8(k): remove "at any time" upon verified noncitizen information
nodes.description: Text-derived process edges: on-rolls → info-received (receipt of documentation or verified information) → removed. These are the only two steps § 8(k) names.

nodes.label: Notice + opportunity to contest before removal (NOT in statute)
nodes.description: Overlay edges (notify, contest, confirm-citizenship) added to the removal table so theorems can state what the statutory text does and does not require. Toggle off to see the statute alone.

nodes.label: lib/lsm — generic labeled state machine (22 theorems, hint-free)
nodes.description: Table-driven lsm-step / lsm-run with once-and-for-all invariants: entry guards, event guards, exit guards, no-skip, closed-set induction, absorbing states, trace composition. Every process invariant in the project is an instance of one of these.

nodes.label: lib/enum_list — enumerated-category algebra (21 theorems, hint-free)
nodes.description: all-in / some-in / none-in / filter over an arbitrary category list, with append, removal, duality and category-widening (statutory amendment) lemmas.

nodes.label: § 8(k) removal process (5 states, 7 edges: 2 statutory + 5 overlay)
nodes.description: Second lsm client. The table is generated from the clause IR; every theorem in removal_invariants.lisp is a library instance discharged by evaluating the table.

nodes.label: Routes back onto the rolls exist only through the overlay (contest) or, in S. 1383, by providing proof after notice
nodes.description: lsm-sources-into (on-rolls) = (contested): the statutory text provides no route back onto the rolls after removal.

nodes.label: lsm-run-entry-guard (library): reaching a target set from outside visits one of its source states
nodes.description: Proved once by induction in lib/lsm. Instantiated for registration (acceptance states), denial (denial states) and removal.

nodes.label: § 8(k) path to removal has no notice or hearing; the S. 1383 SAVE-match path REQUIRES notice
nodes.description: Two results. § 8(k) (both texts): receive verified information → remove "at any time", no notice event. S. 1383 § 8(j)(4)(B) adds a systematic DHS SAVE-match path on which removal is reachable only after the notify event and an opportunity to provide proof.

nodes.label: § 3(b)(5): a birth certificate alone is not proof; with a government photo ID it is
nodes.description: v3–v5 modeled a birth certificate or naturalization certificate as standalone proof. The generated documentary-proof-bundlep follows the statute: supporting documents count only together with an anchor photo ID.

nodes.label: § 8(k): removal is reachable without notice (structural, no legal assumptions)
nodes.description: Neutral structural result: the statutory process admits removal from the rolls with no notice or hearing event. The model does NOT assert this is unconstitutional; it gives a due-process argument a precise mechanical target.

nodes.label: Mathews v. Eldridge (1976)
nodes.description: Procedural due process: private interest, risk of erroneous deprivation, government interest.

nodes.label: Husted v. A. Philip Randolph Inst. (2018)
nodes.description: NVRA list-maintenance procedure upheld.

nodes.label: citizen-b: registered citizen, erroneously flagged, removed without notice
nodes.description: Shared scenario B: citizen-b is a person, citizen, eligible, on the rolls; the State holds (erroneous) verified information of noncitizenship; no notice, no hearing.

nodes.label: § 8(k): statute removes registrant on verified information
nodes.description: Generated text rule: person + on rolls + verified noncitizen information ⇒ the SAVE Act removes the registrant.

nodes.label: Removal without notice or hearing violates due process
nodes.description: Challenger interpretive rule (Mathews): a qualified registered voter removed without notice and hearing suffers a due-process violation; bridge: not a valid regulation as applied.

nodes.label: Removal on verified information is valid list maintenance
nodes.description: Government interpretive rule (Husted): verified information + important interest + evenhanded procedure establish the removal defense, notice or no notice; bridge: valid as applied.

nodes.label: Removal conflict pivots on valid-regulationp as applied to the registrant
nodes.description: Given law, qualified voter, protected right, removal transaction and statutory removal, the removal conflict condition is exactly (not (valid-regulationp law p)).

nodes.label: Challenger: any registered citizen removed on verified info without notice/hearing ⇒ removal conflict
Government: verified info + important interest + evenhanded ⇒ no removal conflict
Challenger: § 8(k) REMOVAL CONFLICT (citizen-b)
nodes.description: Under the challenger's removal premises, ACL2 derives a constitutional removal conflict for citizen-b.

nodes.label: Government: NO § 8(k) REMOVAL CONFLICT (citizen-b)
nodes.description: Under the government's removal premises, ACL2 derives that no removal conflict exists for citizen-b.

nodes.label: A plain REAL ID is not documentary proof of citizenship (§ 3(b)(1) needs "indicates citizenship")
nodes.description: Structural fact from the generated § 3(b) table: real-id is not in any category; only real-id-indicating-citizenship is. REAL IDs are issued to all lawful-status holders; only five states issue enhanced licences that denote citizenship.

nodes.label: S. 1383 — SAVE America Act (House amendment, Feb 11 2026)
nodes.description: Current legislative vehicle. § 2 is the H.R. 22 text (verified verbatim in CI); § 3 adds photo identification to vote (new HAVA § 303A).

nodes.label: citizen-c: registered citizen, no expiring photo ID at the polls, no cure within 3 days
nodes.description: Shared scenario C (8 conceded facts): registered citizen votes in person with ballot-c, presents nothing in the § 303A(c) list, does not cure within 3 days.

nodes.label: § 303A(a)(1)(A): no regular ballot without valid photo ID
nodes.description: Generated text rule: registered voter in person without valid physical photo identification ⇒ the official may not provide a regular ballot.

nodes.label: Uncounted ballot + cannot obtain photo ID without burden = severe burden (as-applied)
nodes.description: Challenger rule (Crawford plurality, as-applied challenges preserved) and bridge: severe as-applied burden defeats validity for that ballot.

nodes.label: citizen-c cannot obtain an expiring photo ID without material burden
nodes.description: Challenger-side empirical premise for scenario C.

nodes.label: Photo ID to vote is a valid evenhanded regulation with an adequate provisional cure (Crawford)
nodes.description: Government rule and bridge: important interest + evenhanded requirement + adequate 3-day cure ⇒ valid for every ballot.

nodes.label: § 303A in-person ballot process (7 states, 8 edges) + valid-photo-ID table (5 types)
nodes.description: Third lsm client; tables generated from the clause IR. A ballot is counted only after valid photo ID or a cure within 3 days; an uncured provisional ballot is rejected.

nodes.label: Functional instantiation: concrete models of both parties' encapsulated theories
nodes.description: Generic theorems about the abstract "defense established" / "burden established" predicates are transferred by :functional-instance to concrete conjunctions of the parties' factors; ACL2 discharges the constraint obligations.

nodes.label: Voting conflict pivots on valid-regulationp as applied to the ballot; a cured ballot is never a conflict
A provisional ballot is counted only if a cure event occurred within 3 days; uncured ⇒ rejected
Registration proof and voting ID are different lists: passport satisfies both; photo ID + birth certificate registers but is not valid photo ID at the polls
Challenger: registered citizen, no valid photo ID, no cure, material burden ⇒ voting conflict
Government: important interest + evenhanded + adequate cure ⇒ no voting conflict for any ballot
Challenger: § 303A PHOTO-ID VOTING CONFLICT (citizen-c)
nodes.description: Under the challenger's voting premises, ACL2 derives a constitutional voting conflict for citizen-c's uncounted ballot.

nodes.label: Government: NO § 303A VOTING CONFLICT (citizen-c)
nodes.description: Under the government's voting premises (Crawford), no voting conflict exists for citizen-c.

edges.description: ACE statements are now generated from the IR for 4 of 8 entries
Only with the overlay: a contested removal can return to the rolls
Scenario B follows the statutory path (no notice event)
If NOT valid as applied to the registrant
If valid as applied to the registrant
Scenario C follows the no-ID / lapse path
If NOT valid as applied to the ballot
If valid as applied to the ballot
